title: Renal Denervation Therapy for Drug-Resistant Hypertension -- Introduction
content: Hypertension remains the single most significant worldwide health problem, affecting about a third of the entire global population and accounting for the largest number of preventable deaths, disproportionately affecting low and middle-income countries. [1] [2] [3] [4] Only about a fifth of affected individuals have their blood pressures well controlled. [5] At least 10% of all patients with hypertension worldwide will have true drug-resistant disease, once secondary causes, medication intolerance, and treatment compliance issues have been excluded. [6] For this challenging group of patients, renal denervation therapy offers a promising, durable, complementary therapeutic option that can significantly reduce elevated systolic blood pressures in at least two-thirds of those treated. [7] [8] [9] [10] [11] [12] [13] [14] [15]

title: Renal Denervation Therapy for Drug-Resistant Hypertension -- Introduction
content: Innervation of the kidneys includes both afferent and efferent fibers of the renal plexus. This plexus is a combination of fibers originating from the celiac plexus, aorticorenal ganglia, the intermesenteric plexus, the lumbar, and the least splanchnic nerves. [16] Nerves from these plexuses attach along the renal artery and vein to enter the kidney. Afferent innervation is essential for the recognition of nociception. Little evidence exists for parasympathetic fibers or activity in the kidney, but anatomical findings include cholinergic axons in the main renal arteries, segmental arteries, and the renal pelvis. [16] [17] [18]

title: Renal Denervation Therapy for Drug-Resistant Hypertension -- Introduction
content: Hypertension is associated with increased renal sympathetic nerve activity, which causes the kidneys to reabsorb more sodium and water, restricts renal arterial perfusion by promoting vasoconstriction, reduces glomerular filtration rate, and raises serum renin levels, collectively increasing blood pressure. [19] [20] [21] [22] [23] [24] [25] [26] [27] Chronic sympathetic overactivity may also result in progressive renal impairment and cardiac hypertrophy. [28] [29] [30] [31] [32] Renal denervation therapy offers a unique, durable, and effective treatment that may help reduce the morbidity and mortality of otherwise uncontrollable hypertension, although cardiovascular outcomes trials are lacking. [7] [9] [33] [34] [35] [36] [37]

title: Renal Denervation Therapy for Drug-Resistant Hypertension -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Renal denervation therapy involves the elimination of the kidneys' efferent sympathetic innervation, primarily by destroying adventitial and adjacent periarterial adrenergic fibers that closely surround all renal arteries, branches, and accessory vessels. [38] [39] [40] [41] [42] [43] The kidney is innervated by the renal plexus, a mixed neural network composed of sympathetic, visceral afferent, and parasympathetic fibers. However, parasympathetic nerves are not found in the renal parenchyma (see Image . Kidney Innervation). [43] [44] Sympathetic input to the kidney is 1 of 3 fundamental mechanisms responsible for the normal regulation of blood pressure, the other 2 being the baroreceptor-mediated response to changes in blood flow and the control of sodium chloride concentration by the macula densa cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus. [45] [46] [47] [48] [49]

title: Renal Denervation Therapy for Drug-Resistant Hypertension -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The sympathetic nerve fibers to the kidneys closely surround all renal arteries and are joined at multiple sites along the length of each vessel. [38] [39] [40] A significant percentage of these nerves (late-arriving nerves) skip over the proximal and middle portions of the main renal arteries or bypass them entirely and join distal branches, segmental vessels, or accessory arteries instead. [38] [39] [40] [55] This explains the need for multiple ablative treatments along the full length of all accessible renal arteries of adequate size (>3 mm diameter), including branches, accessory, and segmental vessels, to achieve relatively complete denervation. [56] The most critical site for renal denervation therapy is the proximal renal nerve bed, which contains the largest concentration of renal sympathetic nerves. [8] [39] [43] However, they may be located farther from the renal artery. [8] [39] [43]

title: Renal Denervation Therapy for Drug-Resistant Hypertension -- Indications -- Patient Selection and Clinical Considerations for Renal Denervation Procedures
content: Drug-resistant hypertension is defined as blood pressure exceeding recommended goal levels despite treatment with maximally tolerated doses of at least 3 antihypertensive medications from different drug classes, including angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers, and a diuretic (typically a thiazide-type). [75] [76] [77] [78] [79] The white coat effect, inadequate dosing, and medication nonadherence or intolerance are common causes of uncontrolled hypertension that is not truly drug-resistant. [80] All causes of secondary hypertension, particularly hyperaldosteronism, which is common in this patient group, must also be excluded. [80] [81]

title: Renal Denervation Therapy for Drug-Resistant Hypertension -- Preparation -- Preoperative Assessment
content: Preoperative assessment for renal denervation therapy begins with establishing an accurate average baseline blood pressure. Patients should record home blood pressure twice daily for at least 1 week or undergo 24-hour ambulatory monitoring, with results averaged to confirm true baseline hypertensive status and exclude white-coat hypertension. [82] [135] In addition, this baseline blood pressure serves as the basis for post-procedure comparisons to assess success. Imaging, eg, a computed tomography angiogram, is recommended to exclude structural causes of renovascular hypertension, eg, renal artery stenosis or fibromuscular dysplasia, and to delineate renal arterial anatomy, including accessory arteries that may influence procedural outcomes and candidacy. [136] [137] [138]

title: Renal Denervation Therapy for Drug-Resistant Hypertension -- Technique or Treatment
content: Renal denervation therapy has proven to be an extremely safe procedure. [164] [165] [166] A pooled analysis of recent randomized sham-controlled trials involving 293 patients demonstrated major adverse events in only 3 patients (1% of all individuals treated). [167] Renal denervation is generally limited to patients with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) above 40 mL/min, reflecting the absence of safety data in patients with significant renal functional impairment rather than any increased risk of kidney failure or reduced efficacy. [121] [168] Those with kidney failure and a GFR less than 40 mL/min should ideally enter a clinical trial. Nevertheless, they may be considered for renal denervation therapy on an individual basis if other treatment options are ineffective or unavailable. title: Renal Denervation Therapy for Drug-Resistant Hypertension -- Technique or Treatment -- Common Factors in Performing Renal Denervation Therapy Procedures
content: Patients with extremely high blood pressures may require continuous intravenous sodium nitroprusside or nitrate infusions to maintain hemodynamic stability during the procedure. Unfractionated heparin provides anticoagulation, targeting an activated clotting time greater than 250 seconds. Clinicians generally employ a standard femoral access approach, advance a 0.035-inch guidewire, and position a 6 French pigtail catheter. The catheter tip is placed over the interspace between the first and second lumbar vertebrae for an aortogram to identify accessory renal vessels arising from the aorta. Significant renal failure may prompt omitting the aortogram, though doing so may leave accessory vessels unrecognized. An internal mammary or renal double-curve catheter typically supports renal arterial access and engagement of the main renal arteries and clinically relevant accessory branches.

Impedance variations of 10 to 20 Ω or more signal device instability and require repositioning, while an impedance drop greater than 10% is expected during ablation. High-impedance readings reflect good wall contact but may also indicate placement in a smaller vessel or a side branch. Smaller arterial branches carry a higher risk of electrode overheating, which triggers automatic device shutdown. Cooling improves when 2 or even 3 electrodes are deactivated. After initial treatment, previously switched-off electrodes can be activated to complete therapy.

The device measures 6 French and advances over a 0.014-inch guide wire, which is introduced through a 7- or 8 French femoral sheath. A standard hemostatic valve attaches to the guide catheter to permit advancement of the ultrasonic denervation device. Only the main renal artery and any significant accessory vessels are treated. Ablation begins distally, just proximal to the first branching or bifurcation of the renal artery.

title: Renal Denervation Therapy for Drug-Resistant Hypertension -- Technique or Treatment -- Ultrasonic Renal Denervation Therapy
content: The ultrasonic transducer does not directly contact the arterial wall. Balloon sizes accommodate arteries measuring 3.5, 4.2, 5, 6, 7, and 8 mm in diameter, and a 5 mm radiopaque marker centered on the balloon shaft assists with precise positioning. Balloon pressure remains minimal and is automatically controlled. Treatment settings are automatically adjusted based on balloon size to optimize sympathetic nerve disruption. Sterile water, continuously cooled and circulated through the balloon, preserves arterial wall cooling before, during, and immediately after therapy. [194] Each treatable artery typically undergoes 2 or, optimally, 3 separate 7-second ablative sonications. [195] After a short cooling interval, the balloon automatically deflates, enabling repositioning for additional treatments. Multiple balloon sizes may be required for arteries of varying diameters.

title: Renal Denervation Therapy for Drug-Resistant Hypertension -- Technique or Treatment -- Alcohol-Mediated Denervation
content: Alcohol-mediated renal denervation uses chemical neurolysis to ablate sympathetic renal nerves supplying the major renal arteries and clinically significant accessory vessels. title: Renal Denervation Therapy for Drug-Resistant Hypertension -- Technique or Treatment -- Alcohol-Mediated Denervation
content: Dehydrated alcohol injected into the perivascular space produces chemical neurolysis of the renal sympathetic nerves. A 7 French guiding catheter supports device placement. Treatable vessels measure 3 to 7 mm in diameter. The treatment catheter positions the target treatment zone at the arterial midpoint and at least 1 cm from the renal parenchyma. The device deploys 3 microneedles (0.008 inch), spaced 120 degrees apart, which penetrate approximately 3.2 mm into the arterial adventitia and perivascular space. Renal denervation involves injecting 0.6 mL of dehydrated alcohol into the adventitia and perivascular tissues, with a maximum total dose of 2.4 mL per patient. Accessory vessels meeting the 3 mm or greater diameter requirement may be treated using the same technique.

title: Renal Denervation Therapy for Drug-Resistant Hypertension -- Technique or Treatment -- Radial Artery Approaches For Denervation Therapy
content: Radial artery approaches for renal denervation therapy are in development. This strategy offers several advantages, including reduced access-site complications, lower bleeding risk, improved patient comfort, earlier postprocedural mobility, no additional capital investment, and easier anatomical access. The technique also provides a viable alternative for patients with peripheral artery disease, limited femoral artery access, or elevated bleeding risk. [128] [203] Catheters designed for radial access must be longer (156 cm compared to the standard femoral length of 117 cm) and narrower than those used for femoral access. They may require additional operator training and expertise. This approach is most suitable for smaller, shorter patients.

content: Device-specific approaches vary , as follows: The radiofrequency device is designed to deliver multiple bilateral ablations (4 to 12) to all significant accessible renal arterial branches outside the renal parenchyma, as well as to the main and any accessory renal arteries measuring greater than 3 mm in diameter. title: Renal Denervation Therapy for Drug-Resistant Hypertension -- Clinical Significance -- Hypertension is a Major Worldwide Health Problem
content: Hypertension represents a major global health concern, affecting one-third of the entire adult population or an estimated 1.56 billion individuals worldwide, with about two-thirds in low and middle-income countries, and its prevalence continues to rise. [1] [2] [3] [4] The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that 46% of those affected are unaware they even have the disorder, and less than half (42%) receive treatment. In contrast, only a minority of affected patients have controlled hypertension. At least 10% of all known hypertensives will have true drug-resistant high blood pressure, defined as elevated blood pressure despite at least three separate antihypertensives at maximum tolerable doses after secondary causes have been excluded, or patient noncompliance with treatment that is not correctable. [6] These are the patients who could primarily benefit from denervation therapy.

content: High-quality, patient-centered care relies on clear roles, coordinated communication, and a shared strategy among all professionals involved in the management of hypertension. Clinicians must integrate evidence-based guidelines, screening pathways, and shared decision-making into individualized care plans. Nursing and support staff contribute through blood pressure monitoring, procedural preparation, and patient navigation, while pharmacists ensure medication adherence and identify interactions. Interprofessional teams review outcomes, refine screening criteria, and uphold program standards recommended by national societies. By strengthening collaborative care frameworks, enhancing clinician expertise, and improving access to renal denervation where appropriate, healthcare teams can reduce hypertension-related complications, improve safety, and elevate overall patient outcomes.
